newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM's party heads towards split.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM's party heads towards split.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party appeared headed for a split on Sunday as a faction backing the party's controversial leader threatened to break away and boycott organisational elections later this week.

Backers of Janata Dal chief Laloo Prasad Yadav, indicted in a $280-million corruption case, said they would boycott the party's internal elections on July 3 after a federal court removed Yadav's nominee from a panel of observers supervising the polls.

Yadav and 55 others have been indicted in a scandal over alleged misuse of animal welfare funds. Yadav, who says he is innocent, has refused to step down as chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar.
"We will boycott the party elections since it is being conducted on the basis of fake voter lists," state Janata Dal chief Kamal Paswan told reporters in the Bihar capital Patna.
"Let the party break. The onus for breaking the party would not rest on Yadav but on the central leaders including the prime minister."

Yadav's refusal to quit as Bihar chief minister has embarrassed Gujral, who assumed power two months ago at the head of a fractious 15-party coalition. The Janata Dal is the biggest party in the centre-left alliance.
Last week, a court rejected Yadav's plea for anticipatory bail, or protection against arrest, in connection with the case.
Yadav's supporters in Bihar have made veiled threats to resort to violence if he were arrested. Security has been strengthened in many parts of the state.

Political analysts said a split in the Janata Dal would weaken the ruling coalition, and could play into the hands of the Congress party, which provides make-or-break support to the government without holding any portfolios.
But they said the government was not ready to fall.
"The split will weaken the central government. But the breakaway faction has a way to go before becoming a part of the Congress or any other party," independent analyst Rasheed Talib told Reuters.
